Security review of everything landed since the 2026-07-28 audit — nine findings, all fixed.

**A mitigation that was recorded as shipped had never actually run.** Android's `execSQL` refuses any result-returning statement, so a PRAGMA has to go through `query()`. But `query()` returns a *lazy* cursor: the statement is compiled eagerly — a syntax error still throws, which is why this looked like it worked — and only executed when the cursor is stepped. Every PRAGMA in `ReticulumDatabase` was issued as `query(...).close()`. So `PRAGMA secure_delete = ON`, which is the whole of the 2026-07-28 M4 remediation and the thing that zeroes freed pages so superseded private-key bytes cannot be recovered from the database file, was never applied on any build that shipped it. Neither were the two `wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE)` calls, which means the last-known-good backup could be a copy of a main file missing everything still sitting in the WAL. Fixed with a helper that steps the cursor, verified by reading the PRAGMA back rather than trusting that issuing it worked, and the one-time cleanup flag is versioned so the purge runs once more now that it does something. Found by the test written for the backup fix below, which failed with the backup still holding an identity that had just been reset away.

**The last-known-good backup kept what you deleted.** It is snapshotted once, at database-open time, and nothing refreshed it afterwards — so resetting your identity left the previous private keys in a full copy on disk, and deleting a conversation left the messages there, for the rest of the session. `secure_delete` and the one-time `VACUUM` operate on the live database and cannot reach a separate file. The snapshot is now rewritten after an identity reset and after either delete path, keeping the invariant that a database with no identity is never snapshotted over a good backup.

**Destination retention could be flooded.** `rrc.hub` and `lxmf.propagation` rows were made exempt from the destination count cap because they announce slowly, correctly, and were losing a recency race they should not have been in. The exemption was absolute — and `appName` is not a trust signal, since it is resolved from the announce's 10-byte `name_hash` and `SHA256("rrc.hub")[:10]` is a public constant. Any peer sharing a transport path can therefore announce as a hub from unlimited self-signed identities, and nothing ever reclaimed those rows. On Android the uncapped discovery query fed all of them into a 2 MB CursorWindow — the exact crash the count cap exists to prevent, and permanent, since startup eviction could not touch exempt rows either. The exemption is now an allowance rather than an infinite one: 256 rows per aspect, an order of magnitude above the 40 hubs measured on a live mesh, with the same tiered order and the same favourite / user-labelled / message-history protections.

**A self-chosen name no longer outranks a locally measured one.** The eviction tiering added on 2026-08-30 kept "operator-named" destinations ahead of anonymous churn — but a display name is whatever the announcer wrote in its own app_data, so a flood of *named* strangers landed beside the user's real named nodes and beat them on recency, defeating the tiering with a one-line change on the flooder's side. Anything our own radio heard at all now outranks anything that merely calls itself something; `rssi` is null on every non-RF transport and cannot be claimed from across a TCP mesh. The number of rows kept is unchanged.

**Relay Chat now treats the hub as untrusted on the receive path too.** `rrc-extensions.md` §2 requires a reaction body to be a single grapheme, and says why: it "keeps a 'reaction' from becoming an unbounded second message body". Only sending enforced it — inbound reaction bodies passed straight through, so a hub could put a short line of arbitrary text into a reaction chip, a surface that deliberately bypasses ordinary message rendering. Now gated on the same check, and dropped rather than falling through to the timeline. The reactions column is bounded too, at 16 distinct emoji and 64 reactors each: on this path the reactor identity is whatever the hub says, so both axes were remote-controlled.

**Hub-supplied strings are bounded.** The message id and the reply/react anchors were bounded; room names and nicknames were not, so either arrived at whatever length a frame allowed and went into a database row, a room key and a notification title. Structural ceilings now apply at the envelope, stored room text and nicks go through the same bound the LXMF store path has had since 2026-07-28, and hub-advertised WELCOME limits are clamped before the app applies them to its own sends — they are the bound on what *we* transmit, so a hub advertising a negative body limit blocks every send and an absurd one invites us to put a megabyte on a LoRa link.

**Also fixed:** room and direct-message notification ids could collide once the message table passed row 19,000, letting one replace or cancel the other; and the reactions column's JSON decoder could not read the escape its own encoder writes.

**Accepted, and now written down where it must hold:** RRC attribution is hub-mediated — a compromised hub can attribute any room message to any identity. What makes that tolerable is that a room line only ever wears a hub-supplied nickname or a bare hash prefix, never a name resolved from the signature-verified contacts table, which would let a hostile hub dress a stranger's words in a trusted contact's identity. That constraint is now recorded at the function that produces the label.

Shared with Android: everything except the Android-only database, backup and notification fixes. Nothing here is device-verified.
